rows.R: Protocol pp. 8, 18, 23: one 1000 mg omega-3 capsule/day (EPA >700, DHA >100 mg), 'intended dose EPA+DHA = 1.0 g per day'; report (abstract, p. 2, eAppendix 2) gives 1412 mg EPA+DHA/day. 1412/1000 = 1.41, above the protocol's 90%-125% tolerance. Retained as a plan-report difference in intervention dose; whether this is a real dose change or a different labeling basis (e.g., measured content) cannot be settled from the documents.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1-2 (text); results supplement (supp3) p. 4; protocol (supp1) pp. 8, 18, 20, 23 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Protocol v7 specifies one 1000 mg omega-3 capsule per day with EPA >700 mg and DHA >100 mg, and p. 23 states an intended EPA+DHA dose of 1.0 g/day; p. 20 gives an acceptable deviation of 90%-125%. The report states 1412 mg EPA+DHA (3:1) daily. 1412/1000 = 1.412, outside 1.25. Other nutrients (selenium 30 ug within 25-55; folic acid 400 within 400-600; calcium 100 within 100-200; vitamin D 20 ug) agree. The difference is real on the face of the documents. L indeterminate because the plan may refer to omega-3 oil mass and the report to assayed EPA+DHA, or the formulation may have changed; no document resolves this. This is an intervention-procedure element rather than an analysis element, which I note as context. Card read after judgment; it did not change my view.

rows.R: Protocol p. 43 (v7, 6 Jul 2017) plans Kaplan-Meier/log-rank/Cox and mixed models for MDD onset and IDS as the primary analyses; the undated SAP (pp. 2-4) and the report use logistic regression for cumulative MDD, Cox as secondary/post hoc, GEE for secondary scores. Report follows the SAP; the protocol-report difference is real but may reflect plan version sequence, which the materials do not establish.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 43; SAP pp. 2-5; main PDF pp. 1, 4, 6, 8; supp3 pp. 18-22 (text extraction, full-text searches for Kaplan, log-rank, mixed model).
rows.rationale: Protocol 10.1 names KM, log-rank and Cox for time-to-MDD with 2- and 4-way analyses, plus mixed models for MDD onset and IDS. The SAP names logistic regression with effect coding as the primary analysis. The report presents logistic regression (primary), Cox (labeled post hoc), and GEE/robust linear models for secondary outcomes. No KM curves, log-rank tests or mixed-model MDD results appear in the main paper or results supplement. The report matches the SAP, so the difference is with the protocol only; the SAP is undated and the protocol version supplied is dated July 2017, so I record version_timing. Card consistent with my reading.

rows.R: Figure 1 (main p. 3, rendered) lists 1451 online exclusions for 'BMI <15 or >40'; eAppendix 1 (supp3 p. 3), the abstract, Methods p. 2 and protocol pp. 16, 29 give the online/eligibility range 25-40 (website check BMI >25). The figure label conflicts with the stated online criterion; the eligibility range itself is clear from the text, so minor. Flow arithmetic is internally consistent (exclusion items sum to 3730; 5965-3730 = 2235).
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 3 rendered at 250 dpi (Figure 1), pp. 1-2 text; supp3 p. 3; protocol pp. 16, 29.
rows.rationale: Rendered Figure 1 reads 'BMI <15 or >40' (not a text-layer artifact). eAppendix 1 states the online tool assessed BMI 25-40; protocol 8.3 says the website checked BMI >25. A <15 cutoff would also be implausible for 1451 of 5965 respondents (24%), and the telephone stage excluded only 18 for BMI <25, both of which favor a typographic error for <25. Sum check: 1451+623+591+566+268+220+11 = 3730; 5965-3730 = 2235, matching the figure. Kept in statistical_results because it is a numeric threshold in a flow display; the intended criterion is unambiguous elsewhere, so minor_presentation.

rows.R: Main p. 4: '392 participants (196 in each of the 4 possible intervention combinations)'. 4 x 196 = 784, not 392. power.prop.test(p1=.20, p2=.30, power=.90) gives n = 391.9 per main-effect arm, i.e., 392 per arm = 2 cells x 196; total 784. 196/0.78 = 251.3, consistent with the 250 per cell target. The printed total is wrong; the per-cell target is clear.
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 4 Sample Size (text extraction); R power.prop.test.
rows.rationale: R: power.prop.test(p1=0.2,p2=0.3,power=0.9,sig.level=0.05) -> n = 391.95 per group. In a 2x2 factorial each main-effect comparison pools two cells, so 392 per arm corresponds to 196 per cell and 784 total. The text calls 392 the participant total while also giving 196 in each of 4 cells (4 x 196 = 784). 196/(1-0.22) = 251.3, matching the stated 250 per combination. The arithmetic contradiction is established; the operative design (250 per cell, ~1000) is clear, so minor_presentation and unlikely downstream impact.

rows.R: Protocol p. 16-17: 30% vs 15% cumulative incidence, 180 per group powered for additive interaction, 20% dropout -> 250 per arm. Report p. 4: 30% vs 20% (33% reduction), 196 per cell for main effects, 22% attrition -> 250 per cell. Different effect-size, power target and attrition assumptions behind the same 250.
rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 16-17; main PDF p. 4 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Protocol 4.4: 'difference of 25%', control 30%, intervention 15%, 180 per group for additive interaction, alpha .05, power .90, 20% dropout. Report: 20% vs 30%, main-effect power, 196 per cell, 22% attrition. For the report's inputs power.prop.test gives 392 per arm (see C004). Planned and reported design assumptions differ in the hypothesized effect and the estimand the trial was powered for (interaction vs main effects).

rows.R: Protocol pp. 8-9, 28 list IDS with MDD incidence as a main study endpoint, and GAD-7/EQ-5D-5L as secondary; SAP p. 2 lists PHQ-9 and IDS as secondary and GAD-7/EQ-5D as 'Other'; report p. 4 calls PHQ-9, IDS, GAD-7 and utility all secondary. rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 8-9, 28, 43; SAP p. 2; main PDF pp. 4, 8 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: IDS moves from a main endpoint (protocol 8.1.1, 10.1) to secondary (SAP, report). GAD-7 and EQ-5D-5L are secondary in the protocol, 'Other' in the SAP and secondary in the report. These are outcome-status changes. Because the report agrees partly with each plan document and the order of protocol v7 and the SAP is undocumented, I record version_timing.

rows.R: Cox time-to-MDD is a protocol primary analysis (p. 43) and an SAP secondary analysis (p. 4), but the report labels it post hoc (p. 4, Table 2). Effect modification by site and MDD history is an SAP secondary analysis (pp. 4-5), but main p. 8 calls eAppendix 10's site/history moderation analyses post hoc. Planned analyses carry post hoc designations; the labeling is disclosed in the report but conflicts with the plan.
rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 43-44; SAP pp. 4-5; main PDF pp. 4, 6-8; supp3 pp. 18-20 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The report designates the Cox analysis and the site/history moderation analyses as post hoc although both appear in the supplied plans. This changes the stated prespecification status of analyses the reader is given. The SAP planned effect modification within the primary logistic model; eAppendix 10 shows moderation tables only for 12-month PHQ-9, overall GAD-7 and utility (site), with a one-line statement for MDD history, so the planned primary-outcome site interaction is not shown either. L substantive_difference describes the change in status; it is not a judgment of impropriety.

rows.R: SAP p. 4 plans a sensitivity analysis of additive interaction (RERI from a linear odds model with likelihood-based CIs) for the primary outcome. No RERI or additive-interaction result appears in the main article or results supplement (searched RERI, additive, excess risk); only the multiplicative interaction OR is reported (Table 2).
rows.evidence: SAP p. 4; main PDF pp. 4, 6-7; supp3 pp. 18-22 and full-text search (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Planned primary-outcome sensitivity analysis not reported in any supplied report document. The protocol p. 16 also states the trial was powered for additive interaction, which reinforces that this was a planned element. Retain.

rows.R: SAP p. 5: 'sensitivity analyses will be conducted and reported' for the MAR assumption behind multiple imputation of the primary outcome. Report sensitivity analyses (main p. 4/8; eAppendix 11) are GEE without imputation for secondary outcomes only; CACE (eAppendix 12) addresses adherence, not missingness. No primary-outcome missing-data sensitivity analysis is reported.
rows.evidence: SAP p. 5; main PDF pp. 4, 6, 8; supp3 pp. 21-22 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Searched the main article and results supplement for sensitivity, complete case and imputation analyses. The only missingness sensitivity analysis concerns PHQ-9, IDS, GAD-7 and utility. The primary MDD outcome (23% dropout before 12 months or MDD onset) has no reported MAR sensitivity analysis. Retain as an unreported planned analysis.

rows.R: eAppendix 7 (supp3 p. 15) says the CACE estimate is the ITT effect divided by the complier proportion. ITT MDD ORs (Table 2): supplements 1.06, therapy 0.93; CACE ORs (eAppendix 12): 0.84 and 0.78. Dividing log(1.06) by any c in (0,1] cannot give OR < 1; exp(log(0.93)/0.713) = 0.90, not 0.78. The stated method does not yield the printed MDD CACE estimates, and the supplement OR reverses direction; the therapy CACE OR 0.78 is cited as significant in main p. 8 and Discussion.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 6-9; supp3 pp. 14-16, 22 (text extraction); recalculation in R.
rows.rationale: Compliance for therapy from eAppendix 8: 71.9% and 70.7% (mean ~0.713). exp(log(0.93)/0.713) = 0.903; exp(log(1.06)/0.77) = 1.079. Printed CACE 0.78 and 0.84. For the continuous outcomes the same ratio roughly reproduces CACE (e.g., GAD supplement 0.14/0.77 = 0.18, printed 0.18; IDS supplement 0.36/0.77 = 0.47, printed 0.47; GAD therapy -0.24/0.713 = -0.34, printed -0.31), so the MDD values are the outliers. A latent-class logistic SEM need not equal a rescaled ITT log-OR (non-collapsibility, different conditioning), which is why I use probable rather than confirmed; but a sign reversal of the supplement effect is hard to reconcile with any instrumental-variable CACE built on an ITT OR above 1. Substantive because the therapy CACE OR is a headline secondary finding. Card's bounds agree with mine.

rows.R: eAppendix 10 Table B (supp3 p. 19): site rows Spain 0.107 (-0.424 to 0.520), UK 0.117 (-0.371 to 0.638), Germany 0.058 (-0.401 to 0.606) have CI midpoints 0.048, 0.134, 0.103; the six other rows are centered exactly (e.g., -0.107 vs midpoint -0.107). The printed P values (.694, .637, .804) fit the printed B with the CI-implied SE (P = .66, .65, .82) better than the midpoints, so the site CIs appear misprinted. Nuisance covariates only.
rows.evidence: Supp3 p. 19 (text extraction; table columns checked against Tables A and C); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: midpoint=(L+U)/2, SE=(U-L)/3.92; Spain mid 0.048, SE 0.241, P(b)=.657, P(mid)=.842; UK mid 0.134, SE 0.257, P(b)=.649; Germany mid 0.102, SE 0.257, P(b)=.821. Supplement, F-BA, history, baseline GAD and both interaction rows are centered to 0.001. Linear-model coefficients from Rubin-pooled MI have symmetric Wald intervals, so the site tuples are internally inconsistent. Site coefficients are adjustment terms and not interpreted, so minor_presentation, unlikely downstream impact. Also noted: baseline GAD-7 P printed as '0'.

rows.R: Protocol p. 12 (3.9.8): HAM-D relapse criterion is score >=18 AND a mean absolute increase of 5 points relative to RCT entry; psychosis criterion adds SADS severity >=3; durations 'preferably' 1 week. Report p. 4 lists HDRS >=18 and SCID-rated psychosis without these qualifiers. The stated primary-outcome definition differs; whether conduct differed or the report abbreviated is not shown.
rows.evidence: Protocol (supp1) p. 12; main PDF pp. 1, 4, 6-7 incl. Table 3 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The relapse components in the report omit the +5 point increase condition and the SADS severity threshold that the protocol attaches to the HDRS and psychosis criteria. At RCT entry HDRS could be up to 15 (near remission), so >=18 alone requires only a 3-point rise, a looser definition than >=18 plus +5. This is a difference in the stated primary outcome definition. The report may have shortened the description, which I cannot verify, but the Codebook treats a primary-outcome definition difference as a typical substantive difference.

rows.R: Protocol p. 10 names HOMA as 'the primary measure of glycemic function' and plans BMI/waist alternatives to weight and a secondary weight analysis accounting for depression-related weight loss; p. 16 plans Intent-to-Attend covariate models for attrition. Report (main pp. 1-10, eFigures 1-9) gives glucose and HbA1c, waist and weight models and pattern-mixture models, but no HOMA, BMI, weight-loss-adjusted or Intent-to-Attend results. Report states it covers Aims 1-2 (p. 2).
rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 10, 14, 16; main PDF pp. 2, 4-9; supp2 pp. 1-10 (text extraction; searched HOMA, insulin, BMI, intent-to-attend, premorbid).
rows.rationale: Searched every supplied report page. Premorbid weight appears only in the adverse-weight-gain definition and Table 1, not in a weight-change analysis. Pattern mixture models are reported (p. 5), but the second planned attrition approach (Intent-to-Attend) is not. HOMA, which the protocol calls the primary glycemic measure, has no reported counterpart (insulin is never mentioned). The report scopes itself to Aims 1-2 and refers to other aims being published separately; that does not cover these planned weight and metabolic analyses. Retain as planned analyses not reported.

rows.R: Protocol p. 15: non-metabolic adverse events counted in participants who did not meet the criteria at ACUTE-phase baseline, plus a week-8-onwards tabulation. Report p. 4: UKU adverse effects defined as change from RCT baseline; incident akathisia requires Barnes 0 at RCT baseline. Reference baseline for AE incidence differs; no week-8-onward results reported.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 15; main PDF pp. 2-4, 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Different baseline (acute phase entry vs randomization) changes who counts as having an incident adverse event, so the reported AE incidences are not the planned ones. The planned 'week 8 onwards' AE tabulation and orthostatic hypotension and SSI-based events are also not reported. Retain.

rows.R: Protocol pp. 14, 16: for safety analyses (H2, weight/metabolic) subjects are classified by medications actually taken during protocolized treatment ('regulatory approach'). Report p. 4 states analyses included all randomized participants, and the metabolic models and eFigures 1-8 are by randomized group. Planned as-treated classification vs reported randomized-group classification.
rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 14, 16; main PDF pp. 3-4, 7-8 (Table 4); supp2 pp. 1-9 titles (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Figure 1 shows 5 olanzapine and 2 placebo participants did not receive treatment as randomized, so the classification rule could change group membership for safety analyses. The report does not present an as-treated safety analysis. Retain as an analysis-population difference.

rows.R: Protocol p. 14 (H2): metabolic data after a new/changed lipid-lowering treatment are excluded from the mixed model. Report p. 5/7: main metabolic models include all data; the exclusion (extended to hypoglycemic agents; statins changed in 12, hypoglycemics in 3) is a post hoc sensitivity analysis with results described only as 'qualitatively similar'. Disclosed as post hoc in the report.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 14; main PDF pp. 1, 5, 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The planned primary specification for the metabolic models became a sensitivity analysis, and the abstract's metabolic estimates come from the unrestricted models. The report discloses the analysis as post hoc; disclosure does not remove the plan-report difference. No numerical sensitivity results are reported.

rows.R: Original SAP p. 17 and final SAP p. 58: 'We will also report relative risks in each substratum, using relative risk regression' for the anatomical-location subgroups. Report (abstract; pp. 4-6, Table 2; results supplement eTables) gives risk differences and ORs from logistic regression only; no RR regression output. L left blank: the counts needed to compute crude RRs are printed, so I do not grade the importance.
rows.evidence: Supp3 (SAPs) pp. 17, 58; main PDF pp. 1, 4-6; supp1 contents and eTables (text extraction, searched 'relative risk').
rows.rationale: Planned effect measure for the prespecified subgroup analysis not reported. Subgroup counts (6/18 vs 14/22; 58/78 vs 42/76) are in Table 2, so a reader can derive crude RRs, but the planned regression-based RR estimates are absent. Retained as a planned output not reported; L optional and left blank.

rows.R: Final MOP/protocol v4.5 (Jan 2017) p. 80, scanned page OCR'd: treatment success requires 'no periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid injections after the first 90 days of follow up'. Report p. 3 primary-outcome definition lists inflammation control, prednisone/drops and no safety/intolerability failure, but not the injection criterion; p. 6 reports 4+4 patients with late injections as protocol deviations without saying how they were scored. Original protocol (p. 15, OCR) lacked the criterion.
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 15, 80, 81 (no text layer; OCR at 300 dpi with RapidOCR); supp3 pp. 70, 72, 81; main PDF pp. 3-4, 6 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The final protocol's primary composite contains a late-injection component that the report's enumerated definition omits. The final SAP (Mar 2017) instead treats late injection as a major protocol deviation with a sensitivity analysis based on inflammation at the time of injection, so the plan documents themselves differ. Whether the 8 late-injection patients were counted as failures in the primary analysis is not stated. Primary-outcome definition difference: substantive_difference (description only).

rows.R: SAP 3.5 (orig. p. 28; final p. 69) commits to reporting four missing-data methods (regression MI, longitudinal GLMM, success/failure assignment, complete case) plus hot-deck MI; 3.3.1 (pp. 22, 62) plans a tipping-point analysis for lost patients; final 3.5.1 (p. 70) adds an injection sensitivity analysis. Report gives complete-case primary and one MI sensitivity analysis (p. 7) only.
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 22, 28-29, 62, 68-70, 81; main PDF pp. 4, 6-7 (Figure 2); supp1 eTables (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Searched the main article and results supplement: no GLMM, best/worst-case, hot-deck, tipping-point or injection-time sensitivity result. The SAP explicitly says 'We propose to report the results from all of the following methods'. Retained as planned primary-endpoint robustness analyses not reported.

rows.R: SAP 3.2.3 (pp. 21, 61-62) Aim 2 primary analysis: logistic regression with rescue group and reason for first-drug failure, and per-group success probabilities with 95% CIs 'presented regardless'. Report (p. 4; Table 2 switching row; p. 7) uses the primary 6-month model (treatment fixed, site random) and gives 20/29 vs 7/20 with RD and OR CIs, but no failure-reason adjustment and no individual-group CIs.
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 21, 25, 61-62, 66; supp2 pp. 72-73; main PDF pp. 4, 6-7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Planned covariate (reason for failure) absent from the reported rescue model, and the planned group-specific success probability intervals are not reported. Retain as a model/output difference for the Aim 2 primary analysis.

rows.R: Table 2 / p. 6: missed doses 4.6% (SD 1.0) vs 4.3% (SD 0.5), n = 96/98, Welch t test (p. 4), P = .87. Welch: t = 2.63, df = 139, P = .009. Even at the half-unit extremes most favorable to the null (diff 0.2, SDs 1.05/0.55) P = .10. P = .87 would need an SE of ~1.8 for the 0.3-point difference. Printed summary statistics and P value are incompatible; which is wrong cannot be determined.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 4, 6 (Table 2 and narrative), p. 7 Figure 2 (text extraction); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: se = sqrt(1.0^2/96 + 0.5^2/98) = 0.1138; t = 2.634; Welch df = 139.1; P = 0.0094. Treating the values as SEs gives P ~ .79, still not .87. The adherence test population may differ slightly from 96/98 (enrolled 107/109), which does not change this materially. SDs of 0.5-1.0 percentage points around means of 4-5% missed doses are also implausibly small for a skewed adherence measure. Substantive because the inference about between-group adherence (no difference vs a difference) depends on which element is wrong, and adherence supports the per-protocol sensitivity analysis.

rows.R: SAP 4.1 (orig. p. 31; final p. 71): per-protocol population excludes major protocol deviations and patients receiving <50% of study drug. Report p. 6 and Figure 2 footnote e: per-protocol model includes patients who missed <20% of doses (i.e., >80% received), with no mention of excluding major deviations (n = 184).
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 31, 71-72; main PDF pp. 6-7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Different adherence cutoff (50% received vs 80% received) and different exclusion criteria define a different per-protocol population. Retain.

rows.R: eTable 9 (supp1 p. 15), switching groups: mycophenolate column N = 20, serious systemic diarrhea '1 (3.4)'. 1/20 = 5.0%; 3.4% = 1/29, the methotrexate denominator. Other entries in the same column use N = 20 correctly (e.g., allergic reaction 1 (5.0), fever 1 (5.0)).
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 15-16 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: 1/20 = 0.050; 1/29 = 0.0345. The percentage uses the wrong denominator. The count is unambiguous, so minor_presentation, unlikely downstream impact.

rows.R: SAP Aim 2 (orig. pp. 25-27; final pp. 66-68): availability table gives B/A 58.3 enrolled (55.4 complete) and A/B 38.9 (36.9); with N0 = 108, r1 = .9: 108x.9x.6 = 58.32, 108x.9x.4 = 38.88. The power table assigns 58 to 'Drug A, then Drug B' and 38 to 'Drug B, then Drug A', i.e., swapped sequence labels, and uses enrollment rather than the formula's r2-adjusted completers. Power values reproduce with 58/38 (87.4%); with 55/36 power is 85.6%. Labeling slip; design inference unchanged.
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 25-27, 66-68 (text extraction; formula region checked in text); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: pw = pnorm(|p1-p0|/sqrt(p1(1-p1)/n1 + p0(1-p0)/n0) - 1.96). Rows: (58,38,.42,.15) 0.874; (58,38,.42,.17) 0.802; (58,38,.15,.42) 0.829; (58,76) 0.941; (116,38) 0.955; (40,40) 0.800; (58,38,.40,.15) 0.823 (printed 80%). (55.4,36.9,.42,.15) 0.861. The sequence-heading swap and the use of n before Aim 2 attrition are internal plan inconsistencies, but the power conclusions change by at most ~1-2 points and the reported rescue analysis does not depend on them. minor_presentation.

rows.R: SAP (orig. p. 27; final p. 67): 'approximately 80% power to detect a difference of 17% if the probability of success with mycophenolate mofetil is 0.42'. The matching table row is .42 vs .17 (difference .25) with 80% power, and the summary (p. 68) says 'a difference of 25%'. Recomputed power .42 vs .17, n 58/38 = 0.802; .42 vs .25 (a literal 17-point difference) = 0.43. The '17%' is the rescue probability, mislabeled as the difference.
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 26-27, 67-68 (text extraction); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: 0.42 - 0.17 = 0.25. The table and summary are internally consistent at 25 points; the sentence's '17%' conflicts. Clear slip with the intended meaning recoverable from adjacent text: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Final protocol v4.5 Table 3 (p. 81, OCR) and p. 136: serious = AST/ALT >=5x ULN, leukocytes <=1000/uL. Report Table 3 (p. 8) and eTable 1 (supp1 p. 5): serious = AST/ALT >5x ULN, leukocytes <1000/uL; nonserious leukocytes >1000. Exact boundary values (5.0x ULN; 1000/uL) are classified differently (and 1000/uL falls in neither report category). Boundary-only difference.
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 81, 136 (scanned; OCR at 300 dpi), p. 16 (original protocol); main PDF pp. 3, 6-8; supp1 p. 5 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The difference is confined to values exactly at the cutoffs, which affect safety-failure classification in the primary composite only if a patient's value was exactly 5.0x ULN or 1000/uL. Real but small: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Original protocol p. 3: 'Each non-surgical patient will be matched ... to five (5) surgical patients'. Report (abstract; p. 3 Figure 1 caption; p. 4): each surgical patient matched to 5 nonsurgical patients; 2287 surgical, 11 435 controls (= 5 x 2287). Protocol p. 6 refers only to '1:5 matching'. The plan sentence reverses the direction; given the counts, the reversed direction could not have been implemented, so this reads as a wording slip in the plan.
rows.evidence: Supp2 (protocol) pp. 3, 6, 7; main PDF pp. 1, 3-4 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: 5 x 2287 = 11 435, matching the report. The protocol's literal allocation (5 surgical per control) is the opposite of the report's. The difference is real in the documents but the intended design (1 surgical : 5 controls) is clear from the protocol's sensitivity section and the counts, so minor_presentation.

rows.R: Table 2 (main p. 7, rendered): ARD = control minus surgery per footnote a. Primary 47.7-30.8 = 16.9 (printed 16.9), secondary 10.6 (10.6), mortality 7.8 (7.8) reproduce; heart failure 18.9-6.8 = 12.1 (printed 12.9), CAD 3.7 (4.2), cerebrovascular 1.5 (1.8), nephropathy 10.2 (11.1), AF 5.7 (6.5). Gaps of 0.3-0.9 points exceed one-decimal rounding (max 0.1). eTable 5 repeats the same group risks.
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 7 rendered at 200 dpi (Table 2), p. 4 methods; supp1 p. 7 (eTable 5) (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Rounding of two one-decimal inputs can move the difference by at most 0.1. The five non-reproducing rows are exactly the individual outcomes analyzed in reduced risk sets (No. at risk < full cohort), suggesting the ARD point estimates may come from a different population or computation (e.g., bootstrap means) than the displayed cumulative incidences, but nothing in the report says so. ARDs are extractable effect estimates, so substantive with direct downstream impact.

rows.R: Cerebrovascular ARD 1.8 (95% bootstrap CI -0.03 to 3.4) includes 0 while the adjusted Cox HR 0.67 (0.48-0.94), P = .02. Table 2 footnotes attribute these to different analyses: unadjusted Kaplan-Meier 8-year risk difference with percentile bootstrap CI vs fully adjusted HR over all follow-up. Different estimands, so no contradiction. (The '-0.03' precision is odd but immaterial.)
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 4, 6-8 (Table 2 rendered, Figure 3D); supp1 p. 9 eTable 6 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: An unadjusted 8-year absolute risk difference and an adjusted hazard ratio need not agree on null exclusion. The report's statement that surgery was associated with 'significantly lower incidence' of cerebrovascular events relies on the HR P value, which is consistent with Table 2. Explained by different methods: exclude.

rows.R: Protocol p. 4 lists coronary 'Other' codes (ICD-9 411.X, 411.X AND 414.X ...) without any diagnosis-position condition; report eTable 1 (supp1 p. 2) sets 411.X / 414.X in bold with footnote 'Bolded text indicates it must be a primary diagnosis' (bold spans confirmed from PDF font data). The protocol also says 'see eTable 1 for diagnosis codes/definitions', which could incorporate the primary-diagnosis rule, so the materials cannot tell whether this was a change.
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 4, 7; supp1 p. 2 (text and font-span extraction); main PDF pp. 2, 7.
rows.rationale: The printed plan list and the report's code table differ in a component of the coronary outcome definition (primary-diagnosis restriction). Because the plan itself defers definitions to an eTable 1 whose plan-time content is not supplied, L indeterminate.

rows.R: Protocol p. 4 AF ICD-10 codes: i48.0, i48.2, i48.91. Report eTable 1 (supp1 p. 2): i48.0, i48.1, i48.2, i48.91. The report adds i48.1 (persistent AF) to an outcome that is a primary-composite component and a secondary end point. The plan's pointer to eTable 1 leaves open that the plan-time table already included it.
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 4, 7; supp1 p. 2; main PDF pp. 2, 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Explicit code-list difference in an outcome definition; adding persistent AF codes can only add events. Recorded as a substantive (descriptive) difference in outcome definition, with the caveat about the eTable 1 reference noted.

rows.R: Protocol p. 6: 95% CIs where applicable and no multiplicity adjustment for secondary endpoints; weight and HbA1c to be 'evaluated over time'. Report eTable 8 (supp1 p. 12) gives Bonferroni-corrected 98.8% CIs for all 52 longitudinal metabolic, nutritional and medication contrasts (disclosed in the table heading); main text p. 7 quotes 95% CIs for the 8-year weight and HbA1c differences. L left blank: the protocol's no-adjustment rule names secondary endpoints, so whether these longitudinal analyses fall under it is unclear.
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 6-7; supp1 p. 12; main PDF pp. 4, 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Reported interval level (98.8%, Bonferroni, consistent with 1 - .05/4 = .9875) differs from the planned 95% level. Disclosed in eTable 8. Note also that main text p. 7 labels the 8-year between-group weight difference 20.3 kg as '95% CI, 20.1-20.6' and HbA1c 1.1 as '95% CI, 1.0-1.2', whereas eTable 8 gives the same estimates with '98.8%' intervals (-20.6 to -20.0; -1.2 to -1.0); the interval label differs between locations (observed, not adjudicated).

rows.R: eTable 8 hemoglobin year 5: -0.1 (98.8% CI -0.2 to 0), P < .001. With one-decimal display, an estimate of -0.14 with CI -0.24 to -0.04 prints as -0.1 (-0.2, 0) [-0.04 rounds to -0.0], has symmetric half-width 0.10, z = 0.14/(0.10/2.51) = 3.5, P < .001. The printed values are compatible after rounding.
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 12 (text extraction); hand recomputation with 98.8% critical value 2.51.
rows.rationale: For P < .001 one needs |est|/half-width > 3.29/2.51 = 1.31; values within the half-unit display intervals (est in [-0.15,-0.05], lower in [-0.25,-0.15], upper in [-0.05,0.05]) satisfy this, e.g., -0.14/0.10 = 1.4. The apparent null inclusion is a display artifact ('0' for a small negative endpoint). Explained by rounding: exclude.

rows.R: eTable 12 (supp1 p. 20): rare-outcome E-value E = 1/HR + sqrt(1/HR(1/HR-1)) reproduces all 7 nonprimary rows (e.g., mortality HR .59 -> 2.78, printed 2.81; HF .38 -> 4.70/4.69) but gives 2.66/2.26 for the primary HR .61 (.69), printed 2.15/1.92. The primary values match the common-outcome conversion RR = (1-0.5^sqrt(HR))/(1-0.5^sqrt(1/HR)): HR .605-.615 -> 2.147-2.182; .685-.695 -> 1.893-1.923. So rows use different, unstated transformations, although several secondary outcomes are also common (8-y risk 16-19% in controls).
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 9, 19-20 (text extraction); main PDF p. 7; supp2 p. 7 (amendment); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: E(h) rare-outcome and Es(h) common-outcome as above. The primary E-values are defensible for a common outcome (47.7% at 8 years), so the primary row is not wrong in itself; the issue is the undisclosed mix of methods across rows. Under the common-outcome conversion the secondary E-values would be lower (e.g., mortality 2.24 vs 2.81; heart failure 3.29 vs 4.69; nephropathy 3.16 vs 4.46), which weakens the supplement's robustness interpretation for those end points. probable_issue because the authors' intended method is not stated; I indeterminate because the effect is on a sensitivity metric whose interpretation is qualitative. My view differs from the card in that I locate the problem in the nonprimary rows rather than the primary pair.

rows.R: Plans (protocol p. 13; SAP pp. 5, 9-10): primary end points are CVD incidence and weight change (weight at Y1 in the SAP timeline); diet adherence scores (17-item er-MedDiet, MEDAS) and nutrient intake are 'other intermediate outcomes'. Report (abstract; pp. 2-4) designates 12-month er-MedDiet change as 'the primary end point for this interim analysis' and weight/waist as secondary risk-factor outcomes. Disclosed in report as an exploratory interim analysis (p. 2).
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1-4 (text extraction); protocol (supp1) pp. 13, 31, 38; SAP (supp2) pp. 5, 9-10.
rows.rationale: Outcome status differs: an intermediate outcome is promoted to primary for this report, and a trial primary end point (weight change) is reported as secondary. The report discloses that it is an interim exploratory analysis; disclosure does not remove the plan-report difference.

rows.R: Protocol p. 52: 'All analyses will be performed on an intention-to-treat basis'; SAP p. 13: ITT, each participant remains in the allocated group. Report (Figure 1; p. 4): principal analyses exclude 291 randomized participants (53 without baseline FFQ, 238 with energy intake outside 500-3500/800-4000 kcal/d), and the same restricted set (n = 6583) is used for weight and other risk factors (eTable 9).
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 52; SAP p. 13; main PDF pp. 3-4; supp3 p. 23 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Energy-intake filtering is reasonable for nutrient analyses, but applying it to weight and other non-dietary outcomes departs from the planned ITT population (6874 randomized vs 6583 analyzed). 28+25 = 53; 106+132 = 238; 6874-291 = 6583, consistent with the report.

rows.R: SAP p. 26: 'Main analyses will be based on an intention-to-treat approach with completers only. As sensitivity analysis ... multiple imputation'. Report p. 4 and Table 2 header: principal analyses use multiple imputation of all included participants; completers-only analyses are labeled post hoc sensitivity analyses (eTables 3-5; Figure 1). Roles of the two analyses are reversed (and the planned sensitivity analysis is called post hoc).
rows.evidence: SAP pp. 13, 26; main PDF pp. 3-5; supp3 pp. 9, 23 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The analysis designated as principal differs from the plan. SAP p. 13 lists both as ITT analyses, but p. 26 fixes completers as main. Retain.

rows.R: SAP p. 26: chained-equations MI, 20 imputations, predictors incl. leisure-time PA, baseline BMI and weight, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, family history, household second member, education. Report p. 4: iterative MCMC (Stata mi), 8 imputations, predictors sex, age, smoking, education, BMI, physical activity, group, energy intake and baseline value. Method, number of imputations and predictor set differ.
rows.evidence: SAP p. 26; main PDF p. 4; supp3 p. 24 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Imputation model differences are analysis-specification differences for the reported principal analysis. Retain.

rows.R: Planned for weight change (SAP pp. 25-26; protocol p. 52): covariate-adjusted models (center, sex, age, education, smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, family history, physical activity), subgroup analyses (sex, age, education, diabetes, MetS criteria, smoking, obesity, baseline er-MedDiet), and a sensitivity analysis excluding second household members. Report gives only unadjusted mixed-model changes and proportions with >=5% loss (pp. 4, 8-10; Figures 3-4; eTable 9); none of the planned adjusted, subgroup or household analyses.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 52; SAP pp. 5, 9, 25-26; main PDF pp. 4, 8-10; supp3 eTables 3-9 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Weight change is a trial primary end point with a Y1 assessment in the SAP. The report presents it as a secondary outcome without the planned adjusted, subgroup and sensitivity analyses. The interim, exploratory framing is context, not a reason to exclude.

rows.R: SAP p. 12: for secondary outcomes (27, including waist change) report nominal 95% CIs and, as ancillary analyses, Bonferroni-adjusted (1 - alpha/27) CIs. Report p. 4: 'no additional adjustment was conducted to adjust for type I error'; waist (p. 8; eTable 9) shown with nominal 95% CI only. Planned ancillary adjusted intervals absent. L blank: ancillary output; I do not grade its importance.
rows.evidence: SAP pp. 9, 12; main PDF pp. 4, 8; supp3 p. 23 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Planned ancillary multiplicity-adjusted intervals for a secondary outcome are not reported. For a 1-year interim report the 27-outcome family is largely not yet assessable, which may explain the omission, but the plan-report difference remains for waist.

rows.R: Table 3 (main p. 7), total alcohol %E, between-group 12-month change -0.2 (95% CI -0.4 to 0.1), P = .01. Allowing every displayed value its half-unit, a symmetric Wald interval centered on the estimate gives P between .12 and .33, so P = .01 is impossible with this interval. The 6-month row -0.2 (-0.4 to 0), P = .01 is reconcilable (feasible P .009-.14). Sensitivity analyses give 12-month intervals excluding 0 (eTable 5 completers -0.3 [-0.4 to -0.1], P = .01; eTable 8 -0.2 [-0.3 to -0.1], P = .01), suggesting a lost minus sign on the main upper limit, but the main row as printed is contradictory (rendered and checked: '0.1' is positive).
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 7 Table 3 alcohol rows rendered at 250 dpi; pp. 4, 8; supp3 pp. 15, 22 (text extraction); R grid search over display intervals.
rows.rationale: R: grid over est in [-0.25,-0.15], lower in [-0.45,-0.35], upper in [0.05,0.15] with center = estimate (tolerance 0.0005), z = |est|/((U-L)/2/1.96). 12-month: min P = 0.117, max P = 0.327 vs printed .01. 6-month: min P = .009, max .14, contains .01. The 12-month interval and P disagree on whether the null is excluded, so a reader cannot tell whether the alcohol reduction is significant: confirmed and substantive for that (exploratory) row.

rows.R: eTable 2 (supp3 p. 7): red wine baseline, intervention median (IQR) '33 (0, 29)' g/week: a median cannot exceed the 75th percentile. Control is '4 (0, 29)', suggesting a typographic error (e.g., 3).
rows.evidence: Supp3 p. 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Median 33 > Q3 29 is impossible. Baseline descriptive value for a minor food item; minor_presentation, unlikely downstream impact.

rows.R: eFigure 2 (supp3 p. 26, rendered 220 dpi): in every pair the printed percentage labels are interchanged relative to the bars and legend (e.g., MUFA: intervention bar ~77%, labeled 72%; control bar ~72%, labeled 77%; fat: intervention ~32-33% labeled 34%, control ~34% labeled 32%). For sugary desserts the labels 59%/58% do not match the bars (~68% intervention, ~59-60% control) under either assignment.
rows.evidence: Supp3 p. 26 rendered at 220 dpi and read visually; main PDF p. 8 narrative.
rows.rationale: Bar heights, CIs and P annotations are consistent with the main-text statement that intervention participants more often achieved favorable changes, but the numeric labels assign the larger value to control in 6 of 7 pairs, and the sugary-dessert intervention value is not printed at all. Anyone extracting the printed percentages would reverse the group values: substantive, direct.

rows.R: Protocol v4 p. 30: acute respiratory failure requires >=2 criteria incl. 'respiratory rate > 25 breaths/min during at least 2 hours' and signs of increased work of breathing/fatigue. Report p. 4 (secondary outcome 'postextubation respiratory failure'): respiratory rate >25/min with no duration, and 'clinical signs suggesting respiratory distress'. The stated definition of a secondary outcome differs; whether conduct differed is not shown.
rows.evidence: Protocol (supp1) pp. 25, 30; main PDF pp. 1, 4, 8 (Table 2); supp2 p. 2 eTable 1 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Dropping the 2-hour duration requirement broadens the respiratory-failure criterion. The report may be abbreviating, but its explicit definition differs from the plan's. Described as a substantive difference in an outcome definition.

rows.R: Protocol 6.2-6.3 (pp. 33-34): Cox regression with backward selection giving adjusted HRs for reintubation, and Cox models for ICU, hospital, day-28 and day-90 mortality. Report (pp. 4, 6-8; supp2 all pages) uses chi-square, Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and an adjusted logistic OR; no Cox model or HR is reported (searched 'hazard', 'Cox').
rows.evidence: Protocol pp. 33-34; main PDF pp. 1, 4, 6-8; supp2 pp. 1-9 (text extraction and search).
rows.rationale: Planned Cox analyses for the primary outcome and for mortality are not reported in any supplied report document. Retain.

rows.R: Protocol p. 33: multivariable logistic model with all variables associated at p < .20 plus literature-forced variables, simplified stepwise to p < .05 and forced variables. Report p. 4: logistic model adjusting for the stratification variable (PaCO2) and baseline variables unbalanced at P < .05; only chronic lung disease entered. Covariate-selection rule differs; report says analyses followed 'a predefined statistical analysis plan', which is not supplied.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 33; main PDF pp. 4, 6 (Table 1 footnote), 7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The adjusted primary model's covariate selection (imbalance-based) differs from the protocol's outcome-association-based stepwise rule. The separate SAP the report cites could reconcile this but is not in the package, so the difference stands on the supplied documents.

rows.R: Protocol 6.4 (p. 34): prespecified subgroup analyses of primary and secondary outcomes by underlying cardiac or respiratory disease and by weaning test (T-piece vs minimal pressure support), in addition to PaCO2. Report (p. 4, 7; Figure 3; supp2 eTables 2-4) gives only the PaCO2 subgroup; cardiac/respiratory disease and weaning test appear only as baseline characteristics.
rows.evidence: Protocol p. 34; main PDF pp. 4, 7-8; supp2 pp. 1, 3-7 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Two planned subgroup families for the primary outcome are absent from every supplied report document. Retain.

rows.R: eTable 2 (supp2 p. 4), hypercapnic columns: ineffective cough 14/45 (69) and 16/59 (73); abundant secretions 20/46 (57) and 23/61 (62). Computed: 31.1%, 27.1%, 43.5%, 37.7%. The printed values equal 100 minus the correct percentage (68.9, 72.9, 56.5, 62.3). Counts are right: they add with the nonhypercapnic columns to Table 1 (51+14 = 65/284; 70+16 = 86/322; 101+20 = 121/288; 91+23 = 114/326).
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 3-5; main PDF p. 6 Table 1 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: 14/45 = 0.311, 16/59 = 0.271, 20/46 = 0.435, 23/61 = 0.377. Printed percentages are complements. Counts reconcile with the main table, so the intended values are recoverable from the same cells; baseline descriptive subgroup data. minor_presentation, unlikely downstream impact.

rows.R: Original protocol (pp. 11, 17, 19): primary = % change in urine ACR to year 4; eGFR change secondary; composite of albuminuria progression, eGFR loss >=12 mL/min, ESRD or death. Addendum (pp. 31-32; submitted 3/2015, implemented 2/2016): primary = eGFR change to year 5; composite = >=40% eGFR loss, ESRD or death. Report (pp. 1-4, Table 3) follows the addendum and discloses the change (p. 2). Disclosed, documented amendment; retained as a plan-report difference relative to the original protocol.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 4, 11, 17, 19, 31-33; main PDF pp. 1-4, 9 (text extraction; main pp. 7-9 rendered).
rows.rationale: Outcome hierarchy and composite definition changed between the original protocol and the report; the report matches the dated addendum and discloses the change. Per the fixed review decision, disclosed changes are retained with 'disclosed' noted.

rows.R: Protocol (pp. 4, 11, 12 Table 1): eligibility men >=60, women >=65 years. Report p. 2: parent trial enrolled men >=50 and women >=55 years. The addendum (pp. 31-33) does not address eligibility. Different age thresholds for the analyzed population.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 4, 11-12, 31-33; main PDF p. 2 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Population eligibility differs by 10 years in the lower age bound. The report's thresholds match the parent VITAL trial as conducted, so the protocol likely reflects earlier VITAL plans, but the supplied plan and report differ.

rows.R: Protocol pp. 12, 14: exclude persons with diabetes diagnosed before age 30 'and first treated with insulin'. Report p. 2: exclude diabetes diagnosed before age 30 'treated with insulin for more than 20 years'. Different exclusion rule for presumed type 1 diabetes.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 12, 14; main PDF p. 2 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The two rules identify different people (initial insulin treatment vs >20 years of insulin). Eligibility difference; retain.

rows.R: Protocol p. 14 (IV.c): randomization by the parent trial, stratified by 5-year age group, blocks of 8. Report p. 2: blocks of 8 stratified by age, sex and race. Addendum silent.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 14, 31-33; main PDF p. 2 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Randomization stratifiers differ (sex and race added). Randomization was performed by the parent trial, which may explain the difference, but the supplied plan and the report disagree.

rows.R: Protocol p. 17 Equation 1 (Stevens 2008 creatinine-cystatin C equation: 177.6 x SCr^-0.65 x CysC^-0.57 x age^-0.20 ...) defines eGFR; the addendum (p. 32) does not name an equation. Report p. 3: eGFR by the CKD-EPI creatinine-cystatin C equation (ref 19), with harmonized cystatin C. The estimator of the primary outcome differs from the one in the supplied plan.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 17, 30 (ref 145), 32; main PDF pp. 3, 11; supp2 pp. 2-4 (eAppendix) (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Different eGFR equations give different values and slopes; this is a measurement-definition difference for the primary outcome. Updating to CKD-EPI is a reasonable choice, but it is not documented in the supplied plan.

rows.R: Report p. 3 and Table 3 footnote a call 'time to doubling of urine ACR to a final ACR >=30 mg/g' part of a prespecified secondary outcome. Addendum (p. 32) lists change in ACR (continuous) as secondary, with no categorical ACR outcome; the original protocol (p. 17) used the same 100% increase + >=30 mg/g definition only as one component of a composite that the addendum replaced. Partial plan basis, so L indeterminate.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 17, 32-33; main PDF pp. 3-4, 9 (Table 3 rendered) (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The categorical ACR analysis is described as prespecified, but the operative plan does not contain it as a standalone outcome; its definition derives from a superseded composite. Whether this counts as prespecified depends on which plan version is taken as governing.

rows.R: Plan (protocol p. 19 VI.g; addendum p. 33 15g): adherence analyses restricted to participants reporting (continuous) adherence to >=80% of study medications. Report p. 3 and eTables 1, 5, 8: 'highly adherent' = reporting use of study medications at least two-thirds of the time.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 19, 33; main PDF pp. 3-4; supp2 pp. 6, 10, 13 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Different adherence threshold (80% vs 67%) defines a different sensitivity-analysis population. Retain.

rows.R: Addendum p. 32 (15c): ITT population = 'all participants who return at least one follow-up biosample', with MI for missing year-5 eGFR. Report p. 3: primary analyses include all randomized participants 'regardless of adherence or follow-up' (full analytic population, n = 1312), imputing missing follow-up outcomes; 1090 returned >=1 follow-up blood sample (p. 4).
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 32; main PDF pp. 3-4, 6 (Figure 1), 8 (Table 2 footnotes) (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The report's primary analysis population is broader than planned (adds ~222 participants with no follow-up sample, whose outcomes are entirely imputed). Retain.

rows.R: Addendum p. 32: results from 10 imputed data sets (chained equations) combined by Rubin's rules. Report p. 3: M = 20 imputations. L left blank: the difference is real but technical, and more imputations would not be expected to change estimates materially.
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 32; main PDF pp. 3, 8 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Plan-report difference in the number of imputations for the primary analysis. Retained per the rule that planned-versus-reported analysis specifications that differ are recorded; importance not graded.

rows.R: Addendum p. 32 Equation 2: eGFR = treatment + time + treatment x time + random intercept (no covariates; covariates only in sensitivity analyses if baseline imbalance). Report p. 3 and Table 2 footnote a: primary model adds linear age, sex and their interactions with time, plus baseline urine ACR and its interaction with time; time modeled as 3 categories.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 32-33; main PDF pp. 3, 8; supp2 pp. 9-10 (eTables 4-5) (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The reported primary model is covariate-adjusted, whereas the planned primary model is unadjusted. Retain.

rows.R: Addendum p. 33 (15f): prespecified vitamin D subgroups by baseline total AND bioavailable 25(OH)D, ACR, eGFR and race. Report (p. 3; Figure 3; eFigures 1-2) shows total 25(OH)D, ACR, eGFR, race and BMI subgroups; no bioavailable 25(OH)D subgroup result anywhere. ('Bioavailable' appears only in a conflict-of-interest disclosure, p. 10.)
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 33; main PDF pp. 3, 8-10 (rendered pp. 8-9); supp2 pp. 17-18 (text extraction and search).
rows.rationale: Planned subgroup analysis absent from all supplied report documents. Retain.

rows.R: Allocation: vitamin D active = 370+333 = 703, placebo = 289+320 = 609; omega-3 active = 370+289 = 659, placebo = 653. Figure 3 prints Overall placebo 703 / vitamin D 609, Figure 4 placebo 659 / omega-3 653, and eFigures 2-3 the same (rendered pages). The randomization-group rows are also exchanged (e.g., Figure 3 omega-3-placebo row: placebo 333 / vitamin D 320, but vitamin D + placebo = 333). Mean changes sit in the correct columns (Table 2: vitamin D -12.3, placebo -13.1), so only the counts are exchanged.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1, 5, 6, 8-9 (Figures 3-4 rendered at 170 dpi); supp2 pp. 11, 16, 18-19 (eFigures 2-3 rendered).
rows.rationale: Every forest-plot participant count is assigned to the opposite treatment column across four displays, consistent with a systematic column swap. Subgroup Ns are only available in these displays, so extraction of subgroup sizes would be wrong: substantive, with possible downstream impact; effect estimates themselves appear unaffected.

rows.R: Figure 2 (main p. 7, rendered): panels B and D (omega-3 vs placebo) repeat the vitamin D panel counts exactly (eGFR placebo 607/459/438, active 701/531/496; ACR 609/463/440 vs 702/529/505). Omega-3 counts per Table 2 are 657/499/472 active and 651/491/462 placebo, and per eTable 6 for ACR 658/502/478 and 653/490/467.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 7-8 (Figure 2 and Table 2 rendered at 170 dpi); supp2 p. 11 (eTable 6 rendered).
rows.rationale: The omega-3 panels' participant counts are copies of the vitamin D counts. The correct counts are given in Table 2 and eTable 6, and the box plots' content is unaffected as far as can be judged, so minor_presentation.

rows.R: Protocol p. 15 (V.e.1) and p. 21 (VII.a): '2000 IU (40 ug)' cholecalciferol; p. 21 also gives the UL as '50 ug, or 2000 IU'. 2000 IU / 40 IU per ug = 50 ug, so '40 ug' is a conversion error inside the plan. The IU dose (2000 IU) is consistent everywhere, including the report (p. 2).
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 15, 21; main PDF p. 2 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: 1 ug vitamin D3 = 40 IU; 2000 IU = 50 ug. The plan gives two different ug values for the same IU quantity. The intended dose is clear, and the reported analysis does not depend on the ug figure: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Addendum p. 32: Equation 1 (interaction test) contains vitamin D x t, omega-3 x t and the three-way term but no main time term; Equation 2 (primary) includes beta2(t). As written, Equation 1 would force no change over time in the double-placebo group. Report p. 3 models time with treatment x time terms. Plan-internal model-specification inconsistency; intent is recoverable from Equation 2 and the report.
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 32 (text extraction); main PDF pp. 3-4.
rows.rationale: Omitting the time main effect in a model with treatment x time terms is a misspecification; it is almost certainly a drafting omission, since Equation 2 and the reported model include time. minor_presentation.

rows.R: eTable 2 (supp2 p. 7, rendered): year-5 nonmissing N = 916 overall. Solving all year-5 vitamin D rows for a common split gives active ~491-494 and placebo ~422-425, which reproduces every row except SGLT2 inhibitors: 25/492 = 5.1% (printed 6) and 21/424 = 5.0% (printed 4). The printed SGLT2 percentages cannot both hold with the denominators implied by the rest of the table. Probable rather than confirmed: SGLT2 use was not asked (NA) at baseline and year 2, so a drug-specific response denominator at year 5 cannot be excluded, although the footnote states a common N = 916.
rows.evidence: Supp2 p. 7 rendered at 170 dpi; Python search over denominators x + y = 916.
rows.rationale: Search over x in 300-700 with y = 916 - x, requiring each printed percentage to equal round(100 n/d): for vitamin D, only splits 491/425 to 494/422 fit, and in each SGLT2 is the sole failing row. Fish-oil columns reproduce (e.g., 460/456 fits all rows). Minor descriptive covariate: minor_presentation. Because the SGLT2 item appears only at year 5, its nonmissing count could differ from other items; the footnote's single N argues against this, hence probable_issue.

rows.R: eTable 7 (supp2 p. 12, rendered): title N = 944 and arm Ns 504+440 = 944 and 477+467 = 944, but the footnote says 1311 gave baseline urine, '991 of these also donated a year 5 urine sample and were included', with 320 + 1 excluded (1312 - 321 = 991). Main text p. 4 says 945 provided a year-5 urine sample. The footnote accounting conflicts with the table's analyzed N.
rows.evidence: Supp2 p. 12 rendered at 170 dpi; main PDF p. 4 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: 1311 - 320 = 991, internally consistent within the footnote but not with 944 analyzed (or 945 returned). The table's Ns are unambiguous, so minor_presentation.

rows.R: eFigures 2-3 (supp2 pp. 18-19, rendered): x-axis is the ratio of ACR change, active/placebo; a ratio > 1 means a larger albuminuria increase with the active treatment, i.e., worse. The axis labels put 'Favors Vitamin D' / 'Favors Omega-3' on the > 1 side and 'Favors Placebo' on the < 1 side, the reverse of the ratio's meaning (plan p. 11 and report p. 3 treat slower ACR progression as benefit).
rows.evidence: Supp2 pp. 11, 18-19 rendered at 170 dpi; main PDF pp. 3-4; supp1 pp. 11, 17.
rows.rationale: With ratio = active/placebo for an adverse quantity (albuminuria increase), values below 1 favor the active treatment. The favor labels are reversed, which would lead a reader to misread the direction of subgroup effects: substantive.

rows.R: Initial plan (supp1 p. 4) and final synopsis (p. 19): de novo cancer 'included as an adverse event, not as an outcome'. Final protocol body (p. 25) and change log (p. 45, 2012): de novo cancer moved to a tertiary outcome, separated from secondary and safety outcomes. Report (pp. 2-3; Table 3 p. 8) lists de novo cancer among safety outcomes. The report matches the superseded classification, not the final plan.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 4, 19, 25, 45; main PDF pp. 2-3, 8 (Table 3 rendered at 170 dpi).
rows.rationale: Outcome status differs between the final plan (tertiary outcome) and the report (safety outcome, analyzed per protocol). The final plan documents also disagree with each other (synopsis p. 19 vs body p. 25). Recorded as an outcome-status difference.

rows.R: Plan (SAP 5c, pp. 14, 31; synopses pp. 4, 19): Kaplan-Meier survival curves on ITT. Report (p. 3; Figures 2-3, pp. 6-7): Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard curves; no Kaplan-Meier display. 5-year RFS/OS percentages are given in text. Different descriptive estimator/display for the same ITT survival comparison.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 4, 14, 19, 31, 45; main PDF pp. 1, 3-4, 6-7 (Figures rendered); supp2 searched.
rows.rationale: Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard and Kaplan-Meier survival convey essentially the same information (S(t) ~ exp(-H(t))); the HRs and inference come from the planned Cox model. The difference is real but concerns presentation: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Plan (SAP 5e, pp. 14, 31): 'Relapse and safety outcomes will be evaluated using risk ratio (RR)'. Report: relapse analyzed by post hoc competing-risk subdistribution HR (p. 3, 6; Table 2; Figure 2C); safety outcomes (Table 3) given as counts and percentages only. No RR reported anywhere. L left blank: counts allow crude RRs, so I do not grade the importance.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 14, 31; main PDF pp. 3, 6-8 (Tables 2-3 rendered); supp2 searched.
rows.rationale: Planned effect measure (RR) absent for relapse and safety outcomes. Table 3 percentages recomputed and correct (e.g., 3/227 = 1.3%, 5/147 = 3.4%, 15/166 = 9.0%). Retained as a planned analysis not reported.

rows.R: Final SAP p. 31 and change log p. 45: prespecified subgroups by baseline 25(OH)D low (<20), middle (20-40) and high (>40 ng/mL). Report (abstract; pp. 3-4; Figure 3 caption; limitations p. 8): high group (n = 5) not analyzed and excluded from the interaction test. Disclosed in the report (small sample).
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 31, 45; main PDF pp. 1, 3-5, 7-8 (text extraction; pp. 7-8 rendered).
rows.rationale: A planned subgroup analysis was not carried out; the report discloses and explains this (5 patients). Disclosure does not remove the difference.

rows.R: Table 1 genotype percentages are computed on genotyped patients, not the arm headers: e.g., FokI vitamin D 92/245 = 37.6% (printed 38), BsmI placebo 119/150 = 79.3% (79). Every genotype row reproduces with available-case denominators (one rounding slip: ApaI placebo GT 61/150 = 40.7%, printed 40). The denominators are derivable from the counts; missing genotype numbers are simply not stated.
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 5 Table 1 (text extraction); Python recomputation of all 42 genotype cells.
rows.rationale: Available-case percentages are a valid, conventional calculation and the implied denominators (e.g., 245, 231, 230 vitamin D; 157, 150, 148 placebo) are recoverable by summing the rows. Not stating the number missing is a completeness point, not a numerical error. Exclude. (ApaI 40 vs 40.7 is a trivial rounding slip, noted only.)

rows.R: Table 2 footnote a (main p. 7, rendered): 'HR values greater than 1 indicate that vitamin D supplementation was associated with a decreased probability of the outcome.' The text (p. 6) and Figures 2-3 treat HR < 1 as lower risk with vitamin D (e.g., subdistribution HR 0.44 = 'significantly lower' relapse; Figure 3A HR 0.46 with vitamin D curve below placebo). The footnote reverses the direction for every row of the table.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 3-4, 6-7 (Table 2 and Figures 2-3 rendered at 170 dpi).
rows.rationale: With vitamin D vs placebo Cox models, HR < 1 means fewer events with vitamin D, as the narrative and figures show. The footnote states the opposite. A reader relying on the table footnote would reverse every estimate in Table 2: substantive, possible downstream impact (the narrative makes the intended direction recoverable).

rows.R: Main p. 6: age-adjusted HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.43-0.99), P = .048. Imposing an exact log-symmetric Wald interval on the rounded limits (L in [.425,.435), U in [.985,.995), HR = sqrt(LU) in [.655,.665)) gives P between .043 and .047, so a strict Wald reconstruction misses .048 by less than .001. Such a small gap is expected if the P value came from a likelihood-ratio or score test, and the interval (upper limit 0.99 < 1) and P < .05 agree on significance. Not a reportable inconsistency.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 3, 6 (text extraction; p. 6 rendered); R grid recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: grid over L and U in their display intervals with HR = sqrt(L*U) restricted to [.655,.665); P = 2*pnorm(-|log HR|/SE), SE = (log U - log L)/3.92; P range 0.0428-0.0473 (HR range 0.655-0.658). A looser symmetry tolerance (|log-mid - log HR| < .002) admits P up to .048. Neighboring same-page tuples reproduce within rounding (0.76 [0.50-1.14] -> P .19 vs .18; 0.46 [0.24-0.86] -> .017 vs .02). The residual gap of <0.001 in P is within differences between Wald and other Cox-model tests, and there is no disagreement about null exclusion. I therefore exclude; the card's strict Wald bounds are correct as arithmetic but do not, in my view, establish a reporting error.

rows.R: E changed from protocol_report to plan_material. Protocol v1.5 §3.4 and §6.1 (pp. 11, 22) and §7.1 (p. 28) name sensitivity of the quantitative FOBGold test as the primary endpoint; §3.9 (pp. 13-14) and §7.2 (p. 28) describe the 'primary endpoint' as sensitivity AND specificity AND AUC of both tests. The SAP (§3.2, §5.4-5.5, pp. 6, 8) and the report (pp. 1, 3) both use quantitative-test sensitivity as primary and specificity/AUC as secondary. The conflict lies within the protocol; the report matches the governing SAP and the protocol's own endpoint sections.
rows.evidence: Supp1 (protocol) pp. 11, 13-14, 22, 28; supp2 (SAP) pp. 6, 8-9; main PDF pp. 1, 3-4 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: The day-3 (protocol) vs 'day 2 after intake' (report/SAP) wording is equivalent (day 1 = intake day). The only real discrepancy is the broader parenthetical primary-endpoint wording in two protocol paragraphs (one in the power section), contradicting the protocol's formal endpoint lists. Because the report agrees with the SAP and the formal endpoint lists, I classify this as a plan-internal inconsistency whose intended meaning is clear: minor_presentation. Separately, AUC and likelihood ratios (planned secondary) are not reported, which the report discloses (p. 3); I note this but it is not the candidate's stated discrepancy.

rows.R: Primary composite: 211/989 vs 233/987. Main text/abstract/Table 3/Figure 2 report 'risk ratio 0.93 (0.83-1.04)'; eFigure 12 (supp4 p. 42, rendered) reports the same collapsed-composite value as 'Odds Ratio 0.93 [0.83, 1.04]'. Computed: RR = 21.33%/23.61% = 0.90; OR = 0.88. The printed 0.93 (0.83-1.04) is reproduced exactly by P(high PEEP | event)/P(high PEEP | no event) = (211/444)/(778/1532) = 0.936 (Wald 0.839-1.044), i.e., exposure and outcome reversed. The same number is labeled as two different estimands, and is neither.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1, 4, 8-10 (Table 3, Figure 2 rendered at 180 dpi); supp4 p. 42 (eFigure 12 rendered); SAP p. 2; R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: true RR = (211/989)/(233/987) = 0.904; OR = (211*754)/(778*233) = 0.878; reversed ratio = 0.936 with log-Wald CI 0.839-1.044, matching the printed 0.93 (0.83-1.04). The SAP specifies a risk ratio. The primary effect estimate is therefore mislabeled and miscomputed; the conclusion (no significant effect) is unchanged, since the chi-square P (.23) is symmetric, but the extractable effect size is wrong.

rows.R: Abstract (p. 1): hypoxemia difference '-8.6% (95% CI, -11.1% to 6.1%)'. Table 3 (p. 9, rendered): -8.6 (-11.1 to -6.1), P < .001. The abstract's upper limit has lost its minus sign; the abstract interval as printed would include 0, contradicting P < .001.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1, 9-11 (text extraction; Table 3 rendered).
rows.rationale: 5.0% - 13.6% = -8.6 points; a Wald interval of width ~2.5 on each side gives about -11.1 to -6.1. Sign typo in the abstract; the body gives the correct value and P < .001 makes the intent clear: minor_presentation, though an abstract-based extraction would be wrong (possible impact).

rows.R: Protocol v2.6 (pp. 5, 12 §7.1.2): secondary endpoints include need for postoperative ventilatory support, ICU readmission and hospital readmission within 30 days, hospital-free days at day 90 and mortality at day 90. Updated SAP (Jan 2018, p. 1) and report (p. 3; supp4 p. 21): severe PPC composite, extrapulmonary complications, intraoperative adverse events, ICU admission, wound healing, in-hospital mortality, hospital-free days. Day-90 mortality and 30-day readmission are not reported; the report follows the dated updated SAP.
rows.evidence: Supp1 pp. 5, 12; supp2 pp. 1-3; supp3 p. 1; main PDF pp. 2-3, 9-10; supp4 p. 21 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Secondary outcome list and mortality time frame differ between the protocol and the report; the change is documented by the updated SAP finalized before database lock. Retained as a plan-report outcome difference relative to the protocol.

rows.R: Every binary 'risk ratio' in Table 3 (and eTable 8, eFigure 12) reproduces exactly as P(high PEEP | event)/P(high PEEP | no event), not as risk(high)/risk(low). Examples: pleural effusion 43/989 vs 21/987: true RR 2.04, printed 1.35 (reversed 1.36, 1.14-1.62); hypoxemia 49 vs 134: true 0.36, printed 0.51 (0.40-0.65); hypotension 313 vs 170: true 1.84, printed 1.43; bradycardia 98 vs 59: true 1.66, printed 1.27; in-hospital mortality 12 vs 5: true 2.40, printed 1.41. All 21 rows checked reproduce the reversed ratio and its log-Wald CI (except mortality CI, see C010).
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 4, 8-10 (Table 3 rendered at 180 dpi); supp4 pp. 29, 42 (rendered); SAP p. 2; R script recomputing 21 rows.
rows.rationale: R (n = 989/987): for each row, reversed ratio = (a/(a+c)) / ((989-a)/(1976-a-c)), SE = sqrt(1/a - 1/(a+c) + 1/(989-a) - 1/(1976-a-c)); printed RR and CI match to rounding in all rows (e.g., ARDS 1.50 [0.85-2.64]; pneumothorax 0.50 [0.09-2.72]). The reversed ratios are attenuated toward 1 relative to the true RRs (pleural effusion 1.35 vs 2.04; hypotension 1.43 vs 1.84). P values (uncorrected chi-square) are symmetric and unaffected. The effect sizes, which readers and meta-analyses would extract, are wrong throughout: substantive, direct.

rows.R: Updated SAP p. 2: time to PPC by Kaplan-Meier curves 'compared with the log-rank tests'. Report p. 4 and eFigure 8 (supp4 p. 38, rendered): Kaplan-Meier curves with a Cox HR 0.88 (0.73-1.06), P = .190; no log-rank P is reported anywhere.
rows.evidence: Supp3 pp. 2-3; main PDF pp. 4, 10-11; supp4 pp. 30, 38 (rendered), 42 (text extraction and search).
rows.rationale: The planned log-rank comparison is replaced by a Cox model test. For a single binary covariate the Cox score test is the log-rank test, and the Wald P would be similar, so this is a difference in the reported test rather than in the analysis' substance: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Updated SAP p. 3: the composite-outcome sensitivity analyses include a clinical-severity-weighted multivariate GEE. eTable 9 (supp4 p. 30) and eFigure 12 (p. 42) report the random-effects, count, common-effect GEE, treatment-component interaction and average-relative-effect analyses, but no severity-weighted GEE; main text p. 4 and p. 10-11 do not mention it.
rows.evidence: Supp3 p. 3; main PDF pp. 4, 10-11; supp4 pp. 30, 42 (text extraction; p. 42 rendered).
rows.rationale: One of six planned sensitivity analyses of the primary composite is not reported. Retain as a planned analysis not reported.

rows.R: Table 2 (main p. 7, rendered): tidal volume first/last hour 0.1 (0 to 0.2), P = .007/.008; respiratory rate last hour -0.4 (-0.7 to 0), P = .02. With one-decimal display, a lower/upper limit printed as 0 can be e.g. 0.03 or -0.04, and the P values are then compatible (e.g., RR last hour: SE ~0.17 from SDs 3.9/3.8; a difference of -0.388 to -0.389 gives an upper limit of about -0.05 (prints as 0) and P of about .025).
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 7 rendered at 180 dpi; hand recomputation of SEs from printed SDs and group sizes.
rows.rationale: Tidal volume: SE = sqrt(1.5^2/989 + 0.4^2/987) = 0.049; a difference of ~0.13 gives CI ~0.04-0.23 (prints '0 to 0.2') and P ~ .008. Respiratory rate: SE = sqrt(3.9^2/989 + 3.8^2/987) = 0.173; differences of 0.388-0.389 give an upper limit >= -0.05 (prints as 0) and P < .025 (prints .02). The feasible window is narrow but nonempty, and the SDs and group sizes behind each row are themselves rounded or subject to missing data. Display rounding explains the apparent conflicts: exclude.

rows.R: Table 2 continued (main p. 8, rendered): monitoring 632/982 (64.9) and 651/984 (67.7); reversal 724/982 (74.3) and 723/984 (75.2). Computed with the printed denominators: 64.4%, 66.2%, 73.7%, 73.5%. The printed percentages equal the counts over the neuromuscular-blockade totals (632/974 = 64.9; 651/961 = 67.7; 724/974 = 74.3; 723/961 = 75.2), while the printed differences (-1.8; 0.2) match the 982/984 denominators.
rows.evidence: Main PDF p. 8 rendered at 180 dpi; hand recomputation.
rows.rationale: Percentages and differences in the same rows use different denominators, and the displayed 'No./total No.' does not match the percentage. Intraoperative process measures; the intended values are recoverable: minor_presentation.

rows.R: Table 3: disseminated intravascular coagulation 1 (0.1) vs 0, 'risk ratio' 2.00 (95% CI 1.91 to 2.09), P > .99. The interval excludes 1 while P > .99. With 0 events in the low PEEP group the true RR is undefined; 2.00 (1.91-2.09) is the reversed ratio (1/1)/(988/1975) with its log-Wald CI (see C004).
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 9-10 (Table 3 rendered); R recomputation (reversed ratio 1.999, CI 1.913-2.089; Fisher P = 1.0).
rows.rationale: Interval and test disagree on the null, and the estimate is not a valid risk ratio for a 1-vs-0 comparison. Single event, so interpretive impact is small: minor_presentation. The underlying cause is the estimand error recorded in C004.

rows.R: Table 3: in-hospital mortality 12 (1.2) vs 5 (0.5), 'RR' 1.41 (0.95 to 1.81), P = .09. The point estimate is the reversed ratio (1.415), but the printed interval does not follow the log-Wald construction that reproduces every other row (reversed-ratio CI would be 1.04-1.93, excluding 1); it is also asymmetric on the log scale (1.41/0.95 = 1.48 vs 1.81/1.41 = 1.28). True RR = 2.40 (log-Wald 95% CI 0.85-6.77). Uncorrected chi-square P = .089 matches the printed .09.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 9-10 (Table 3 rendered); R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: reversed ratio (12/17)/(977/1959) = 1.415, SE = 0.158, CI 1.04-1.93; true RR (12/989)/(5/987) = 2.40. The printed mortality interval cannot be reproduced by the method used for the other rows, and the reported estimate is not the planned RR. Mortality is a prespecified secondary outcome likely to be extracted: substantive.

rows.R: Protocol Appendix iii (p. 31): mild respiratory failure = SpO2 < 90% / PaO2 < 60 in room air but responding to supplemental oxygen; moderate = hypoxemia DESPITE supplemental oxygen. Report (Table 3 note d; supp4 p. 20): mild = responding to <=2 L/min oxygen; moderate = responding only to >2 L/min. The mild/moderate boundary is defined differently, which also moves patients into or out of the severe-PPC secondary composite (which excludes only mild failure).
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 31; supp3 p. 1; main PDF pp. 9-10; supp4 p. 20 (text extraction).
rows.rationale: Under the protocol, a patient who responds to 4 L/min oxygen is 'mild'; under the report he is 'moderate' and counts toward the severe composite. Outcome-component definition difference. Retain.

rows.R: Protocol p. 32 coma definition, rendered at 300 dpi: 'Glasgow Coma Score <= 8' (underlined less-than; text layer shows '<'). Results supplement p. 21: 'Glasgow Coma Score < 8'. A GCS of exactly 8 counts as coma under the plan but not under the report. 2 vs 2 coma events reported.
rows.evidence: Supp1 p. 32 rendered at 300 dpi (glyph checked; extracted text loses the underline); supp4 p. 21; main PDF p. 9.
rows.rationale: Boundary-only difference in one extrapulmonary component with very few events: minor_presentation.

rows.R: eTable 8 per-protocol (supp4 p. 29, rendered): cardiopulmonary edema 15/917 vs 7/912, effect 1.36 (1.02-1.82), P = 0.09. The interval excludes 1 while P = .09 (uncorrected chi-square .089). The estimate and CI are the reversed ratio (1.366, 1.023-1.824; true RR 2.13), so the interval and the chi-square test come from different constructions and disagree on significance.
rows.evidence: Supp4 p. 29 rendered at 170 dpi; R recomputation.
rows.rationale: R: reversed ratio and log-Wald CI reproduce 1.36 (1.02-1.82); chisq.test without correction P = 0.089. The interval/test conflict is real in the printed table. It is a component in a per-protocol sensitivity analysis, so I grade it minor_presentation here; the systematic estimand problem is captured in C004.
